---
title: "Sound 22: The Vocoder"
toc: true
toc-depth: 2
---

A **vocoder** makes an instrument talk. It takes two sounds: a **modulator** (usually a voice) and a
**carrier** (usually a synth playing chords). It measures how loud each band of frequencies is in the
voice, moment by moment, and sets the loudness of the same bands in the synth to match. The synth
keeps its pitch and chords; the voice supplies the words. It's the robot voice of Kraftwerk, Herbie
Hancock, Daft Punk and Laurie Anderson. It was invented at Bell Labs in the 1930s to squeeze speech
down telephone lines.

**How to use the page.** Put on **headphones**: the microphone hears the speakers otherwise. Choose
**Microphone** as the modulator (or the built-in **Robot voice** if there's no mic), press ▶, then talk
or sing while you play chords on the computer keys, the on-screen keyboard or a MIDI keyboard. Until
you play, a chord is held for you.

::: {.sk-care}
The microphone only switches on when you choose it and press ▶ (the browser asks first). The
**🎤 Mic** button in the bottom bar turns it off again. Nothing is recorded or sent anywhere.
:::

## The vocoder

<div class="sk" data-w="vocoder"></div>

## How it works

The vocoder is built from parts you have already met:

1. **Split the voice into bands.** A row of [band-pass filters](sound-filter.qmd), each a different
   frequency from low to high, splits the voice into 16 or so bands.
2. **Measure each band.** An **envelope follower** on each band turns the wobbling band into a smooth
   level: how loud that band is right now. The bars under the controls show those levels.
3. **Split the synth the same way.** A second row of band-pass filters, at the same frequencies,
   splits the carrier.
4. **Let the voice turn the synth up and down.** Each band of the synth is turned up and down by the
   level of the matching band of the voice, and the bands are added back together.

A vowel is a pattern of loud bands (the formants, from the [filter lesson](sound-filter.qmd)), so the
synth takes on the vowel. The pitch comes from the synth, which is why you can speak in a monotone
and have it sing in chords.

## Things to try

- **Bands.** With 4 bands the words are barely understandable; with 16 they're clear; with 32 it
  sounds almost like a voice through a synth-shaped filter. Old hardware vocoders had 8 to 20.
- **Band sharpness.** Higher Q makes each band narrower: more ringing and more "robot".
- **Envelope speed.** Slow (5 Hz) blurs the words into a smooth pad; fast (60 Hz) keeps every
  consonant but gets gritty.
- **Let "s" sounds through.** A synth has little energy in the very top, so "s", "t" and "f"
  disappear. Real vocoders pass the voice's top end straight through to keep the words clear.
- **Carrier.** A sawtooth is best, because it has energy in every band for the voice to shape.
  A square works less well (it is missing every other harmonic). **Noise** as the carrier gives a
  whisper with no pitch at all.
- **Listen to** the modulator or the carrier alone to hear what goes in.
- **Drum loop as the modulator** makes the chord pulse in the rhythm of the drums, a trick used in
  dance music.
